results.title: Relative Risk vs Absolute Risk Reporting
results.content: # Relative Risk vs Absolute Risk Reporting. May 27, 2019, 10:39 AM IST **Dr Philip Lee Miller** in AntiAging, Lifestyle, TOI. I have written often and spoken repeatedly to so many of my patients about relative versus absolute risk. That is the absolute risk reduction is 9 and 1000, which is 0.9%. *Relative risk reduction*: the relative risk reduction is the absolute risk reduction divided by the proportion of patients who die without treatment. The relative risk reduction looks more impressive than the absolute risk reduction. I will quote the results showing relative risk ratios (RR). Pooling the results from the random-effects model showed that low-dose aspirin, compared with control, was associated with an increased risk of any intracranial bleeding (8 trials; relative risk, 1.37; 95%CI, 1.13-1.66; 2 additional intracranial hemorrhages in 1000 people), with potentially the greatest relative risk increase for subdural or extradural hemorrhage (4 trials; relative risk, 1.53; 95%CI, 1.08-2.18) and less for intracerebral hemorrhage and subarachnoid hemorrhage. *Relative vs Absolute Risk Graphic*. What is the difference between relative and absolute risk or statistics with a sample size of 10, 100, or 1,000? This first graphic shows a relative risk reduction of 50% across 3 sample sizes. The large yellow arrow shows an equal risk reduction across these sample sizes. The relative risk reduction is independent of the sample size. Now let’s look at the absolute risk reduction across these 3 sample sizes. The absolute risk reduction (large yellow arrow) becomes almost invisible as the sample size increases. Absolute risk reduction is entirely dependent on the sample size. The study, which looked at 359 papers on randomized trials, found that most researchers furnish a statistic only for “relative risk reduction”–the percentage difference between the effect of the treatment and a placebo. Just 18 included the more straightforward absolute risk reduction. If a treatment reduced the absolute risk from, say, 4 to 1 per cent, it appears more impressive to present only the relative reduction of 75 per cent. Those of you who are followers of Dr Peter Attia have also been treated to this same discussion of risk management, risk analysis, and poor statistical methodology.

results.title: How to explain smoothing functions in the logistic regression model - Cross Validated
results.content: # How to explain smoothing functions in the logistic regression model. I fitted a logistic regression model with some smoothing functions, and the software made beautiful plots for them. My main concern is that there is no reference level in the continuous variable, so converting the estimates by an exponential function to odds ratio seems not quite right for smoothing functions. $\begingroup$ Unless I am misunderstanding your concern (always a possibility), it seems to me the lack of a reference level for Age is irrelevant. The odds ratio that the conversion of the estimates would put out is (probability of the event / (1-probability of the event)) where "event" is determined by the left hand side variable of your regression. All the smoothing function does is generate a smooth, but not necessarily linear, fit to the odds ratio (equivalent to generating a smooth but not necessarily linear fit to the probability.) There's no assumption about a reference Age in there. If you want the reference age to be 18, then just subtract 0.8 from the value of f(age) for every value of age. answered Sep 9, 2013 at 18:49. An additional question is, based on your statement, how to calculate a new confidence interval of a specific age when the reference age is 18-year-old?? To make a 95% CI for the odds ratio with 18 as the reference, you need to find the variance (and thus the std error) of $exp(f(age)-f(18))$ for various values of age. The best way to explain the smoothing model is probably to show a graph and explain it. How exactly I would graph this depends on how many independent variables you have, but I would have the Y axis represent some kind of probability (given that this is a logistic model). answered Sep 9, 2013 at 18:35. results.title: Statistical Calculations on Sampled Data – Online Course
results.content: Statistical Calculations on Sampled Data – Online Course. * Choose between **time-based** vs **sample-based** statistical calculations and understand how they differ, especially with asynchronous signals. You’ll dive into **basic statistics**: calculating RMS, mean, peak values, crest factor, variance, and more, and learn how to set up output channels and choose calculation modes (such as single-value, windowed, or run-based) during acquisition . The course emphasizes understanding **time-based vs sample-based calculations**—highlighting how sample alignment can significantly affect results with asynchronous data, as detailed in Dewesoft’s support documentation. Next, you’ll master **array statistics** to compute metrics over dynamic data blocks, and **classification functions** to tag or count samples meeting defined conditions. * **Sum** provides the total of all acquired values based on the selected calculation type (sample- or time-dependent). Before we discuss the calculation types, it is important to note that the **Block-based** and **Running** calculation types are computed according to the specified time interval or the number of samples. It is important to note that every single sample is used as an input value for the statistical calculations. **Single value, Sample-based calculation:**. If you have only two samples in a measurement with values of 5 and 10, the single-value average for a sample-based calculation will equal 7.5. **Single value, Time-based calculation:**. Single value average of a time based calculation explanation. **Block-based calculation** computes the statistical quantities over a specific time interval defined by the block size. The Triggered Blocks option calculates the statistical value based on a specific trigger event. The Start/Stop Blocks option calculates the statistical value beginning at a specific trigger event. Array statistics can be used to calculate statistical values from the array. The option **Show class as a separate channel** is available only when the **Single value based** calculation type is selected. * **Absolute count** – Each class value represents the number of samples within the class. * **Relative count** – Each class value represents the number of samples in the class normalized to the total number of counted samples. For all options, you must also define **Visualization** – the number of classes for the average value, minimum, and maximum value.

Teiko Dashboard: Log₂ Fold change now available as a baseline normalization method. You can choose how to visualize immune changes in your cytometry datasets with two baseline normalization options: Log₂ Fold Change or Absolute Change. With both baseline normalization options, you can analyze your cytometry data in two powerful, complementary ways:. * Absolute Change - View the raw difference between baseline and on-treatment values (e.g., from 1% to 1.1% = +0.1%). * Log₂ Fold Change - See the relative intensity of change from baseline on a standardized scale (e.g., log₂(2) = 1 for a 2-fold increase). Use them together to explore both magnitude and proportional shifts in immune cell frequencies, giving you a more complete picture of your cytometry data. ### Teiko.
